text: Lesson 13 got Entra ID and AWS talking to each other. This lesson is about doing that in a way that holds up once you're managing dozens of AWS accounts and several Azure subscriptions — the point where multi-cloud stops being two environments and starts being an org chart's worth of them.

The pattern that scales is one identity source of truth, with every cloud federating into it as a relying party. Not Azure having its own identity and AWS having its own identity synced to each other — that's two sources of truth pretending to be one, and it rots the moment a group membership changes in only one place. Entra ID owns who exists and what they're allowed; AWS just consumes that decision.

Concretely, a sign-in can start two ways. IdP-initiated means the user opens Entra ID's app portal and gets sent to AWS with a signed assertion. SP-initiated means they go to the AWS portal first and get redirected to Entra ID to authenticate. Either way, that assertion carries group membership, which AWS IAM Identity Center reads to decide which permission set — its name for a reusable bundle of IAM policies — the user gets, in which accounts, with zero manual AWS console work.

This replaces the older default of an IAM user and access key per person per account — long-lived secrets that rarely get rotated and don't carry any of the context Entra ID already knows. After the SAML assertion validates, IAM Identity Center issues short-lived AWS STS credentials instead. There's no standing secret to leak, and the access only exists because a recent, real sign-in happened — the exact lever Conditional Access uses next lesson.

The same discipline has to hold as you scale: resist the local IAM user created as a shortcut, because every exception is a thread back to the three-directory problem. AWS Organizations plus Identity Center assigns permission sets across many accounts from one place, so a single Entra ID group change reaches everywhere it should.
